job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Erik Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Ortega & Bell, a tax practice in Haverley, by 8:45. I'm a trainee, so I prepare returns for small businesses and farmers, collect documents and sit in on client meetings with Mrs. Bell. I'm doing my professional accountancy exams in the evenings, paid for partly by the firm. I share a flat with two lads from my course, and my loan is 41,000. On Sundays I go to church with my gran in the next village, then I cook for the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a useful tool, not magic. At work I'd tell Mrs. Bell we should use it for first drafts and keep the judgement with us. In church or with my gran I'd say people were scared for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about the job and a bit tight on money. I earn 23,000, the exams cost about 900 a year even with the firm's help, and the loan takes 200 a month. There are only four decent practices within an hour of here, so I'd have to stay and be good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the exams, ask to take on a few clients of my own in the second year, and keep up the evening study. I'd save 50 a month. I'd also keep using the AI assistant for drafts, since I've seen that it saves an hour here and there. And I'd keep going to church for the community, which is what keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. It's the picture where hard work pays off. I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the exams cost 900. How do you cover that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm covers half. I use savings for the rest, and I skip things like holidays. I don't mind, because I see it as an investment in a real qualification. People who've passed these exams don't get laid off easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. A qualified accountant is a name on a form, and regulators want a person. But I'm also aware that's an assumption. If AI changed what a qualification means, I'd feel foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, and the sensible thing is to get good at it and also keep the human side strong. At work I'd say the firm should show clients that a person checks everything. I wouldn't complain about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the trainee job changes a lot. Preparing returns and collecting documents is exactly what the card says gets taken over. But the part where you sit with a farmer and explain the tax bill is another thing. If I can be that person, I think I'm fine. If not, I'm cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into both sides. I'd learn the firm's new tools properly and ask Mrs. Bell to let me take client meetings. I'd keep up the exams, since the qualification is my protection. I'd also volunteer at the church hall's money clinic on Saturdays, to practise explaining money to ordinary people. And I'd save more, maybe 80 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. It's not fear, it's like being on a ladder in the wind. I think I'll be fine, but I'm holding on harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the firm cut trainees anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a bigger firm in the city, or try the tax office. That means leaving my gran, which I'd hate. She's 79 and I go every Sunday. But I'd go if I had to, and I'd drive back every other weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the money clinic really help your career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not. But it helps people in the community, and it gives me practice explaining things plainly. In the long run I think that's what a human accountant is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast, and we should look after each other: families, churches, local firms. I'd also say governments should back apprenticeships and local work, rather than just paying people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my profession is among the first hit. Tax rules are text and numbers, and a machine reads them faster than I will. Qualifications might still matter, but fewer firms will need juniors. With 41,000 of debt and a month of savings, I couldn't wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying for the exams if the firm stopped paying half, and I'd put that money against my loan. I'd look for a trade or an apprenticeship that works with hands, maybe in the electrical or heating line, as robots come later. I'd also look to the church for community help and ask my uncle Jonas, who owns a garage, if I could work there evenings. And I'd talk to Mrs. Bell about what the practice will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'd feel a hole in my stomach. I'm not one to panic, though, so I'd try to make a list and do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop the exams. Isn't that giving up on the qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and it hurts, because I worked for it. But if the work disappears, a half-finished qualification costs 900 a year for nothing. I'd rather put it against the debt. I can come back to it if the world turns out slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your gran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's all in hand. She lived through harder times, and she'd tell me to trust in God and work. I'd listen, and then I'd quietly start looking at jobs on the other side of the county.

say: Two years is too fast, so look after each other: **families**, churches and local firms.
Back **apprenticeships** and local work, not just payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. I'd say people should work hard, learn real skills and not expect the government to fix it for them. But I'd say employers should train their people while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm anxious but have a fair chance. In five years I could finish my exams, clear half my loan and have a good name at the practice. Then it hits, and I'd need to be someone clients trust, not just someone who fills in forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams in about three years, take on my own small client list and become the person people ask for. I'd save 90 a month and overpay the loan. I'd also learn the tools well, since being the one who knows them matters. In year three or four, I'd look into advice for farmers and small firms, which stays personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but determined. It's a bit like running for a train and seeing it's not leaving yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why advice for farmers and small firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they trust people they know, not websites. A farmer will sit with someone from the same area. That kind of trust takes years to build, and I think it's something a machine finds hard to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if that's wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in a field that's gone, and I'd need to move on. But I'd have the exams, a clear loan and a good reputation, and that's more than most. I'd retrain into something else, and I'd be proud of what I did.

say: Five years is a fair **warning**; work hard, learn real skills and don't wait for the government.
Employers should **train** their people while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people use it. I'd say to young people to get a qualification and a trade skill, and to build savings. And I'd say we should keep community together, because that's what holds people up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fairly settled. By 32 I'd be a qualified accountant with my own clients, the loan cleared and probably a wife and a child on the way. The question would be whether the qualification still counts for anything, and I'd keep an eye on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the exams within three years, then become a manager at the practice or start something of my own in the village. I'd clear the loan by 27. I'd marry Lina, my girlfriend, in about four years and buy a small house near my gran's village. I'd keep learning the tools as they prove themselves. And I'd keep teaching Sunday school, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with small worries. I'd feel I could build a normal life, the kind my grandparents would recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lina. Does she share your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. She's a nurse, so she's safer from AI in the near term, and she's keen on a family in about five years. If the two-year picture were real, we'd probably wait. With ten years, we'd go ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ten years turned out to be six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd speed things up and cut costs, and we'd be tight but not wrecked. Having a nurse in the house helps, and I'd have my exams done. That's why I'd keep a cushion, in case the clock moves.

say: Ten years is plenty if people **use** it: a qualification, a trade skill and savings.
Keep **community** together, because it holds people up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years doesn't leave time to finish exams, clear debt or move sensibly, and the exams might not mean much by then. What would help is jobs that reward work, apprenticeships and employers who train rather than cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that I don't want to be a victim. I'm not asking for a handout. I'd like a fair shot at building something with my hands and my head, and to keep my family close.

headlineQuote: I'd like a fair shot at building something with my hands and my head, and to keep my family close.
portrait: **Erik** is 22, a finance graduate working as a trainee at a tax practice in Haverley while doing his accountancy exams.
He owes **41,000**, has about a month saved and shares a flat with two friends.
He is traditional, church-going and steady with technology, using AI **now and then** at work.
He bets on **trust** and qualifications, then turns to trades and family when the clock speeds up.
Time lets him plan marriage and a house; two years makes him **alarmed**.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years leaves no time to finish exams or clear debt.
whatWouldHelp: Jobs that reward **work**, apprenticeships and employers who train people rather than cut them.
